text: On a catch-up call, I told my friend Nick Wignall how someone had trained an AI model to write blog posts in my style. It was a pure research exercise on their part. The idea was to train the tool on my past work, then give it the headlines and opening paragraphs of my posts. Could it generate the rest of each piece in a similar fashion? I only compared a handful of posts from their AI versions to their app versions to their real questions, but I quickly concluded the writing suffered from the same not making the opposite argument. It sounded so on. The creator wanted to know if such a model once it worked properly, of course, could be useful to me. I told him even if it worked perfectly, it wouldn't lie because I don't write a daily blog to crank out a post every day. If that was the point, I'd have switched to AI long ago already. I write a daily blog to make sure I remember how to think. It's a daily practice to my practice, to my practice for my brain, a creative ritual to strengthen my writing muscles, and a reader's commitment to my readers. I promised that I'll show Klein a bit of what Klein said. That's so far. AI hasn't been all that useful to him. He uses it for light research or to structure some data, but that's about it. Why? Because the writer doing the research is what makes the writing unique. When you're using AI as a writer, you're outsourcing the part of the work and that would not need to do the most. Klein believes having AI summarize a book or a paper for me is a disaster. It has no idea when to add to it, what it would mean. So it links in everybody, which I will include in its average emergence of points to you. Nick pointed out the same applies to a writer struggling when creating a piece when you're stuck and sit there thinking, trying to come up with what's next. That's the valuable part of writing. It's tempting to use AI to remove that stuckness, but it's basically cheating and leads to a very different result. AI is great at giving you a list of ideas. You'll almost always find one you can plug in and keep writing, but is it the idea that needs to slot into this gap or just a bad piece of filler of the writing? In a way, I think it'll make it even easier to stand out because the more people take shortcuts, the less quality will remain for readers to flock to, even if the overall quantity of options is much larger. When a technology makes it feel like you can avoid the suck, it's most likely a mirage. The path behind easy only leads to the lowest common denominator. The real artists' fighters' makers these stick with a truth as old as time itself. The suck is why we're here and only those who overcome it themselves will reap holy
